opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think one of the most interesting shifts is that organizations are starting to realize their rules — whether that's an access control policy, a compliance requirement, an HR handbook, or a mortgage eligibility guideline — are actually little logical theories. For a long time those rules lived in natural language documents, and the only way to evaluate them was to have people read them, argue about them, and hope they'd interpreted them consistently.

What generative AI does is lower the cost of getting from that natural language into something formal. You can take a policy document, have a model help translate it into logic, and then use automated reasoning tools — SMT solvers, theorem provers — to ask precise questions. Is this policy consistent with itself? Are there two rules that contradict each other? Is there any situation where someone gets access they shouldn't? Does the new version of the policy allow anything the old version didn't? Those are questions a reasoning engine can answer definitively, with proof, rather than by sampling a few test cases.

And what we've found, going back to our work on things like IAM policies at AWS, is that the moment you formalize the rules, you discover ambiguity. People who thought they agreed on what a policy meant turn out to have quite different interpretations. So the tools don't just check the rules — they force a conversation about what the rules should be in the first place. That's actually where a lot of the value is.

The other piece is that generative AI on its own is not trustworthy enough to be the arbiter. A large language model might give you a plausible answer about whether something is allowed, but it can hallucinate. So the combination is powerful: the LLM handles the messy translation and the user interaction, and the automated reasoning provides the soundness guarantee. You can even turn it around and use the formalized rules to check the LLM's outputs — so when a chatbot tells a customer "yes, you're eligible for this refund," you can verify that answer against the formal policy and explain why it's correct or flag that it isn't.

So I think organizations are moving from a world where rules are things you write down and occasionally audit, to one where rules are artifacts you can query, test, version, and prove things about — much the way we've treated software. And that opens up a lot of new possibilities for how confidently companies can deploy AI in regulated or high-stakes settings.

r001.rationale: It says formal reasoning can check whether a policy is consistent with itself and identify rules that contradict each other.

r002.rationale: It proposes comparing what a new policy allows against the old policy, but does not propose checking how answers to historical customer questions would change.

r003.rationale: It does not propose consulting customers whose answers would change under a proposed rule.

r004.rationale: It says generative AI lowers the cost of translating natural-language rules into formal logic, making automated reasoning tools easier to use.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss NP problems or their practical tractability.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks, Sam. It's great to be here.

So I think the way I'd frame it is that organizations have always run on rules. Access control policies, network configurations, compliance regimes, tax codes, the rules of a loyalty program, whatever it is. And historically the problem has been that those rules live in two places that don't talk to each other. There's the natural language version, the policy document, the regulation, the thing a lawyer or a security officer wrote. And then there's the executable version, the IAM policy, the firewall rule, the chunk of code that actually implements it. And the gap between those two is where most of the pain is. People write a policy in English, somebody else translates it into something a machine can enforce, and nobody really knows if the translation is right.

What's changed with generative AI is that we now have a tool that's really good at crossing that boundary. A large language model can read the English and propose the formal version, or read the formal version and explain it back to you in English. That's genuinely new. Five years ago, if you wanted to take a compliance document and turn it into something a solver could reason about, you needed a specialist, and there just aren't that many of those people in the world.

But, and this is the part I care most about, the model on its own isn't enough. These models are probabilistic. They'll give you something that looks right, that reads plausibly, and sometimes it's subtly wrong. And with rules, subtly wrong is the whole game. An access policy that's ninety-five percent correct is a security incident waiting to happen.

So the combination I find exciting is generative AI paired with automated reasoning. The language model does the translation, the creative part, the part that's hard for machines to do precisely. And then a theorem prover or an SMT solver does the checking, the part that's hard for humans to do reliably. The solver doesn't guess. It gives you a proof, or it gives you a counterexample. If the model proposed a policy that lets the wrong person in under some obscure condition, the solver finds that condition and hands it to you.

And that changes how organizations evaluate rules in a few concrete ways. First, you can ask questions you couldn't ask before. Instead of "does this policy look okay," you can ask "is there any request, in the entire space of possible requests, that this policy allows and the old one didn't." That's a question with a mathematical answer. Second, you can do it continuously, every time something changes, rather than once a year in an audit. And third, the explanations come back in a form a non-specialist can actually read, because the model is sitting there to translate the counterexample into plain language.

I'd also say there's a cultural shift that comes with this. When checking is cheap, people start writing rules differently. They write them to be checkable. They ask what the rule is actually supposed to guarantee, rather than just what it says. And that's healthy, because a lot of rules in organizations have accreted over years and nobody remembers what they were for.

The honest caveat is that you still need to get the specification right. The solver can prove that the implementation matches the spec, but if the spec is wrong, you've just proven the wrong thing very rigorously. So the human stays in the loop, but at a much higher level, thinking about intent instead of chasing down edge cases by hand. That's the shift I see happening.

r001.rationale: The response discusses checking policies and finding counterexamples, but does not say organizational rules can be jointly unsatisfiable.

r002.rationale: It proposes comparing what a new policy allows with what an old one allowed, but does not use historical customer questions for that evaluation.

r003.rationale: It does not propose consulting affected customers about whether changed answers would cause problems.

r004.rationale: It says generative AI can translate between natural-language policies and formal versions, reducing the need for scarce specialists and making reasoning workflows more accessible.

r005.rationale: The response does not discuss NP problems or their practical tractability.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s an opportunity to change rules from something you write down and periodically review into something you can actually ask questions about. Are these rules consistent? Do they allow something we intended to prohibit? If we change this rule, what else changes?

Generative AI can help bridge the gap between the language people use to describe their intentions and the precise language that reasoning tools need. Then the reasoning tools can check the implications and, when something is wrong, produce a concrete example: here’s a situation where your rules permit an outcome you didn’t expect.

The important distinction is that generating a plausible interpretation isn’t the same as establishing that it’s correct. You still need to validate that the formal representation captures what people meant. But once you have that, you can move from checking a handful of examples to making much stronger statements about the rules. That makes the review process much more interactive and, potentially, much more rigorous.

r001.rationale: Asks whether the rules are consistent, clearly raising the possibility that rules can conflict when considered together.

r002.rationale: Does not propose checking how a new rule would change answers to historical customer questions.

r003.rationale: Does not propose consulting customers about the effects of changed answers.

r004.rationale: Says generative AI can bridge everyday descriptions of intentions and the precise language reasoning tools need, making those tools more accessible.

r005.rationale: Does not mention NP problems or their practical tractability.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the opportunity is to make rules something you can actually interrogate. Organizations have policies, regulations, and procedures written in natural language, and it can be difficult to understand whether they’re consistent or whether they produce the outcomes people intend.

Generative AI can help translate those documents into a more precise representation. Then reasoning tools can ask questions like: Can these two requirements be satisfied at the same time? Is there a situation where this policy allows something we meant to prohibit? If we change this rule, what else is affected?

The important distinction is that generating a plausible interpretation isn’t the same as establishing that it’s correct. You still need people to validate that the formal representation captures their intent. But once you have that, automated reasoning can give you a much stronger basis for evaluating the rules—and concrete examples of where they break down.

r001.rationale: It asks whether two requirements can be satisfied at the same time, conveying that organizational rules may be jointly unsatisfiable.

r002.rationale: It does not propose checking how a new rule would change answers to historical customer questions.

r003.rationale: It does not propose consulting customers about answer changes or their effects.

r004.rationale: It says generative AI can translate documents into a precise representation, but does not clearly credit it with making reasoning tools more accessible.

r005.rationale: It makes no claim about NP problems or their practical tractability.
